Aceldama (Field of Blood)
uh-SEL-duh-muh
proper noun (place)
Aramaic Chaqal Dema ("field of blood"), transliterated into Greek as Akeldama (Acts 1:19). The field bought with the thirty pieces of silver Judas received for betraying Christ.

📖 Biblical Definition

Aceldama ("the field of blood") was a field near Jerusalem associated with the thirty pieces of silver that Judas Iscariot received for betraying the Lord Jesus, and with Judas's own terrible end. The Gospels and Acts give complementary accounts. Matthew records that Judas, seized with remorse, brought the thirty pieces of silver back to the chief priests, confessing, "I have sinned in that I have betrayed the innocent blood"; they would not take it back, and Judas cast down the silver in the temple and went and hanged himself. The chief priests, unwilling to put the "price of blood" into the treasury, took the money and bought with it the potter's field to bury strangers in, "wherefore that field was called, The field of blood, unto this day" (Matt 27:3-8) — and Matthew sees in this a fulfillment of prophecy (Zech 11:12-13; Jer 32). Acts adds that Judas "purchased a field with the reward of iniquity; and falling headlong, he burst asunder in the midst, and all his bowels gushed out... and it was called... Aceldama, that is to say, The field of blood" (Acts 1:18-19). The two accounts harmonize: the priests bought the field with Judas's blood-money (so it was "his" purchase, the fruit of his iniquity), and Judas hanged himself, his body afterward falling and bursting open. Aceldama stands as a permanent monument to the wages of betrayal: the field bought with the price of innocent blood, the burial-ground for strangers, named forever "the field of blood." It is bound up with the doom of Judas, "the son of perdition" (John 17:12), who betrayed the Lord with a kiss for thirty pieces of silver (the price of a slave, Exod 21:32), and who went "to his own place" (Acts 1:25). Aceldama testifies that the price of betraying Christ is blood and ruin, and that the silver of treachery purchases only a grave.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The "field of blood" near Jerusalem bought with the thirty pieces of silver Judas received for betraying Christ (Matt 27:3-10; Acts 1:18-19); a monument to the wages of betrayal — the blood-money purchasing only a burial-ground and the doom of Judas.

ACELDAMA (FIELD OF BLOOD), proper noun. Aramaic Chaqal Dema ("field of blood"); Greek Akeldama (Acts 1:19).

The field associated with the thirty pieces of silver Judas received for betraying the Lord.

Judas returned the money confessing he had betrayed innocent blood, then hanged himself (Matt 27:3-5).

The chief priests bought the potter's field with the "price of blood" to bury strangers (Matt 27:6-8).

Acts: Judas "purchased a field with the reward of iniquity" and fell headlong, bursting open (Acts 1:18-19).

📖 Key Scripture

Matthew 27:6-8 — "And the chief priests took the silver pieces, and said, It is not lawful for to put them into the treasury, because it is the price of blood. And they took counsel, and bought with them the potter's field, to bury strangers in. Wherefore that field was called, The field of blood, unto this day."

Acts 1:18-19 — "Now this man purchased a field with the reward of iniquity; and falling headlong, he burst asunder in the midst, and all his bowels gushed out... that field is called in their proper tongue, Aceldama, that is to say, The field of blood."

Matthew 27:3-4 — "Then Judas, which had betrayed him, when he saw that he was condemned, repented himself, and brought again the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and elders, Saying, I have sinned in that I have betrayed the innocent blood."

Acts 1:25 — "That he may take part of this ministry and apostleship, from which Judas by transgression fell, that he might go to his own place."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Aceldama is corrupted when the Matthew and Acts accounts are alleged to contradict, when Judas's remorse is mistaken for saving repentance, or when the monument to the wages of betrayal is read as mere grim history.

expand to see more

Contradiction-alleged misreading. Skeptics claim Matthew (Judas hanged himself; the priests bought the field) and Acts (Judas bought the field; he fell and burst open) contradict each other. They harmonize naturally: the priests purchased the field with Judas's blood-money, so it was in effect "his" purchase, the fruit of his iniquity (Acts speaks of what his money did); and Judas hanged himself (Matthew), his body afterward falling, perhaps when the rope or branch broke, and bursting open on the ground (Acts describes the aftermath). The two accounts are complementary, not contradictory — one describing the means (hanging) and the other the gruesome result (the fall and bursting), one the priests' purchase and the other its source in Judas's money.

Remorse-mistaken-for-repentance misreading. Judas "repented himself" (Matt 27:3) and confessed, "I have betrayed the innocent blood" — yet he is the son of perdition who went to his own place (Acts 1:25). His remorse was not saving repentance. The Greek word for his "repentance" (metamelētheis, regret) differs from the saving repentance (metanoia) that turns to Christ for mercy. Judas felt the horror of his sin and the weight of his guilt, but he turned not to the Savior he had betrayed but to despair and self-destruction. This is the difference between worldly sorrow, which "worketh death," and godly sorrow, which "worketh repentance to salvation" (2 Cor 7:10). Judas's remorse drove him to a noose; true repentance would have driven him to the very Christ he had betrayed, who receives even the chief of sinners. Aceldama is a warning: remorse without turning to Christ ends in ruin.
